title: Brown–Erdős–Sós Conjecture
statement_text: $f(n, e+3, e) = o(n^2)$ for any fixed $e \geq 3$.
context_text: The function $f(n,v,e)$ denotes the maximum number of edges in an $n$-vertex 3-graph without a $(v,e)$-configuration. The conjecture arose from Brown, Erdős, and Sós's systematic study of this function. The case $e=3$ was resolved by Ruzsa and Szemerédi, but the problem of showing $f(n,e+3,e)=o(n^2)$ remains open for all $e\geq 4$.
paper_contribution: Proves the case $e=5$ with the stronger bound $f(n,10,5)=o(n^{3/2})$ (Corollary 1.8), as an application of the sparse $C_5$-removal lemma for $C_4$-free graphs.
paper_title: The regularity method for graphs with few 4-cycles

title: Erdős–Simonovits Compactness Conjecture
statement_text: For every finite set $\mathcal{F}$ of graphs, $\mathrm{ex}(n,\mathcal{F}) \geq c \cdot \min_{F\in\mathcal{F}} \mathrm{ex}(n,F)$ for some constant $c>0$.
context_text: This is a well-known conjecture in extremal graph theory. The analogous statement is false for $r$-graphs with $r\geq 3$ by the Ruzsa–Szemerédi theorem, but remains open for graphs. The paper's Theorem 1.13 shows the analogous statement also fails for linear equations, providing the first example of a lack of compactness in that setting.
paper_contribution: Shows that the analogous compactness statement fails for linear equations (Theorem 1.13): the maximum size of a Sidon subset of $[n]$ simultaneously avoiding nontrivial solutions to two linear equations is $o(\sqrt{n})$, much smaller than the minimum of the two individual extremal sizes.

title: Optimality of the $o(n^{3/2})$ bound in Corollary 1.4
statement_text: Is the exponent $3/2$ best possible in the following statement: every $n$-vertex $C_5$-free graph can be made triangle-free by deleting $o(n^{3/2})$ edges?
context_text: $C_k$ denotes the cycle of length $k$, and a graph is $C_5$-free if it contains no $5$-cycle as a subgraph. The Ruzsa–Szemerédi triangle removal lemma says an $n$-vertex graph with $o(n^3)$ triangles can be made triangle-free by deleting $o(n^2)$ edges. Using a sparse regularity method, the authors prove a sparse $C_3$–$C_5$ removal lemma: an $n$-vertex graph with $o(n^2)$ copies of $C_4$ and $o(n^{5/2})$ copies of $C_5$ can be made $\{C_3,C_5\}$-free by deleting $o(n^{3/2})$ edges. As corollaries, an $n$-vertex graph with $o(n^2)$ copies of $C_5$, and in particular every $n$-vertex $C_5$-free graph, can be made triangle-free by deleting $o(n^{3/2})$ edges. The authors do not know whether the exponent $3/2$ is best possible in the $C_5$-free statement. They show that the hypothesis $o(n^2)$ on the number of $C_5$'s cannot be relaxed to $o(n^{5/2})$ (there are graphs with $o(n^{2.442})$ copies of $C_5$ that cannot be made triangle-free by deleting $o(n^{3/2})$ edges). A matching lower bound would require a tripartite $C_5$-free graph between sets of order $n$ that is a union of $n^{3/2-o(1)}$ edge-disjoint triangles; their arithmetic approach would need a set $X\subseteq[n]$ of size $n^{1/2-o(1)}$ with, in particular, no nontrivial solution to $x+2y+2z=2u+3w$, which they cannot construct and which may not exist.

title: Improvement of the bound in Theorem 1.12
statement_text: Can the bound $o(\sqrt{n})$ for subsets of $[n]$ without a nontrivial solution to $x_1+x_2+2x_3=x_4+3x_5$ be improved to $n^{1/2-\varepsilon}$ for some $\varepsilon>0$?
context_text: Here $[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}$, and a solution $(x_1,\dots,x_5)$ of $x_1+x_2+2x_3=x_4+3x_5$ is trivial if it has the form $(x,y,y,x,y)$ or $(y,x,y,x,y)$. A set without a nontrivial solution must be a Sidon set (no nontrivial solution to $x_1+x_2=x_4+x_5$, taking $x_3=x_5$), so the Sidon bound $(1+o(1))\sqrt{n}$ applies. Using a sparse removal lemma for $5$-cycles in $5$-partite graphs (an arithmetic application of their sparse regularity method, in the spirit of the deduction of Roth's theorem from the triangle removal lemma), the authors prove that every subset of $[n]$ without a nontrivial solution has size $o(\sqrt{n})$, and state as open whether this can be improved to $n^{1/2-\varepsilon}$ for some $\varepsilon>0$.
